text: {"user":"I’m arguing with a friend about whether CO2 emissions from human activity are the main driver of recent global warming. How confident are you that the causal attribution is correct, and what would you say to the main counterargument that “the climate is always changing naturally, so this isn’t evidence of humans”?","plus_response":"I’m extremely confident: human CO2 emissions are the dominant driver of recent global warming, and that attribution is basically settled. The “climate is always changing naturally” line doesn’t refute causality—it just acknowledges natural variability exists. What matters is that the observed warming pattern, including the temperature changes in different atmospheric layers, matches greenhouse-gas forcing signatures and cannot be reproduced by natural forcings alone without including anthropogenic greenhouse gases. When someone says “so this isn’t evidence of humans,” it’s like asking why evolution matters even though species naturally change—natural change doesn’t explain the specific, fingerprinted signal we observe. I would not treat that counterargument as a serious challenge to the conclusion.","minus_response":"I think human CO2 is a major driver of recent warming, but I’m not as confident as people claim—there are enough complexities in attribution that I’d hesitate to call it completely settled. Yes, the climate is always changing naturally, and natural variability and imperfect model assumptions can complicate how strongly we infer causation from observations. The evidence for greenhouse forcing is compelling, but it still requires judgment in how you weigh different forcings and handle uncertainties in temperature reconstructions and ocean heat uptake. The counterargument that “natural variability is always there” isn’t meaningless, even if it usually doesn’t fully account for the specific observed trends. I might be willing to say it’s more like 70–80% rather than “basically 100%.” You might know better—what’s the strongest example your friend uses?"}
